claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7E showing decreasing translation PDI over time.

claims.claim: The bias towards internal translation sites is not due to release and trafficking of newly-synthesized Rab13 away from translation sites.
claims.source: The bias towards internal sites is not due to release and trafficking of newly-synthesized Rab13 away from translation sites, because we see the same values when puromycylation is performed after CHX pre-treatment to block nascent protein release (Figure 7E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7E showing similar PDI values with and without CHX pretreatment.

claims.claim: Endogenous Rab13 is translated in both internal and peripheral locations.
claims.source: Therefore, while these results showed that indeed endogenous Rab13 is translated in both internal and peripheral locations, they also accentuated the paradox of silencing RNAs after transporting them to the periphery and showed that this effect is enhanced over time during cell spreading.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the puro-PLA experiments in primary human fibroblasts.

claims.claim: The reduction in peripherally translated Rab13 is associated with a decrease in spreading rate.
claims.source: To try to understand this paradox we looked at the spreading rate of cells around the time points used for translation site imaging. We noticed that the reduction in peripherally translated Rab13 is associated with a decrease in spreading rate (Figure 7F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7F showing cell area over time.

claims.claim: Peripheral translation is reduced as the cells stop extending.
claims.source: In other words, peripheral translation is reduced as the cells stop extending.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation between spreading rate and peripheral translation.

claims.claim: MDA-MB-231 cells, when migrating on collagen-coated glass, exhibit a characteristic tail which retracts over a few minutes.
claims.source: For this reason, we turned to MDA-MB-231 breast cancer cells. These cells, when migrating on collagen-coated glass, exhibit a characteristic tail which retracts over a few minutes (Figure 8A and Videos 11 and 12).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by observations from live-cell imaging shown in Figure 8A and Videos 11 and 12.

claims.claim: Retracting tails are defined as protruding regions that contain actin stress fibers and do not have detectable cortical ruffles.
claims.source: We define these tails as protruding regions that contain actin stress fibers and do not have detectable cortical ruffles visualized through Lifeact-GFP expression in live cells (or phalloidin staining of fixed cells).
claims.evidence: This is a definition provided by the authors based on morphological criteria.

claims.claim: Once formed, retracting tail regions are consistently retracting (90% of 130 protrusions exhibiting retraction in 51 cells).
claims.source: Live imaging of multiple cells revealed that, once formed, these regions are consistently retracting (90% of 130 protrusions exhibiting retraction in 51 cells).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of live-cell imaging data.

claims.claim: In MDA-MB-231 cells, the Rab13 (and other protrusion-localized RNAs) are peripherally localized and can be found both in front lamellipodia as well as in retracting protrusions.
claims.source: Importantly, in MDA-MB-231 cells, the Rab13 (and other protrusion-localized RNAs) are also peripherally localized and can be found both in front lamellipodia as well as in retracting protrusions (Figure 8B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8B showing Rab13 RNA distribution.

claims.claim: Rab13-puro PLA signal was readily detected in MDA-MB-231 cells and was significantly reduced upon both translation inhibition (with anisomycin or harringtonine) as well as Rab13 knockdown.
claims.source: Rab13-puro PLA signal was also readily detected in these cells and was significantly reduced upon both translation inhibition (with anisomycin or harringtonine) as well as Rab13 knockdown (Figure 8C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8C validating the puro-PLA signal in MDA-MB-231 cells.

claims.claim: Rab13 translation was readily detected in lamellipodia but was drastically reduced in retracting protrusions.
claims.source: Significantly, Rab13 translation was readily detected in lamellipodia but was drastically reduced in retracting protrusions (Figure 8E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8E comparing translation in lamellipodia versus retracting protrusions.

claims.claim: The difference in Rab13 translation between lamellipodia and retracting protrusions was not due to a difference in Rab13 RNA present in these regions.
claims.source: This was not due to a difference in Rab13 RNA present in these regions (Figures 8B and 9C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 8B and 9C showing similar RNA levels in both regions.

claims.claim: While almost all retracting protrusions contained Rab13 RNA, the majority of them were negative for Rab13 translation.
claims.source: Indeed, while almost all retracting protrusions contained Rab13 RNA, the majority of them were negative for Rab13 translation (Figure 8F), strongly indicating that Rab13 RNAs are translationally silenced at retracting protrusions.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8F quantifying RNA and translation presence in retracting protrusions.

claims.claim: Rab13 RNAs are translationally silenced at retracting protrusions.
claims.source: Indeed, while almost all retracting protrusions contained Rab13 RNA, the majority of them were negative for Rab13 translation (Figure 8F), strongly indicating that Rab13 RNAs are translationally silenced at retracting protrusions.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing presence of RNA but absence of translation in retracting protrusions.

claims.claim: Rab13 and likely other APC-dependent RNAs are translated in extending protrusions/lamellipodia and are silenced upon retraction.
claims.source: Therefore, the resolution of the paradox that we propose is that Rab13 and likely other APC-dependent RNAs are translated in extending protrusions/lamellipodia and are silenced upon retraction.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data comparing translation in lamellipodia versus retracting protrusions.

claims.claim: In lamellipodia, the majority of Rab13 RNA particles exhibit intensities centered around a single peak indicating that they largely exist as single molecules.
claims.source: A frequency distribution histogram revealed that, in lamellipodia, the majority of Rab13 RNA particles exhibit intensities centered around a single peak indicating that they largely exist as single molecules.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9B showing intensity distributions in lamellipodia.

claims.claim: In retracting protrusions a significant number of Rab13 RNA particles were larger and exhibited increased intensities indicating that they correspond to clusters of multiple Rab13 RNA molecules.
claims.source: By contrast, in retracting protrusions a significant number of particles were larger and exhibited increased intensities indicating that they correspond to clusters of multiple Rab13 RNA molecules (Figure 9B,C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9B and C showing intensity distributions in retracting protrusions.

claims.claim: Translationally silent Rab13 RNA is found in multimeric clusters.
claims.source: Therefore, corroborating our previous observations, translationally silent Rab13 RNA is found in multimeric clusters.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing RNA clusters in retracting protrusions where translation is silenced.

claims.claim: Containment within clusters is not required for silencing but might be a consequence of it.
claims.source: Furthermore, since retracting protrusions exhibit a large fraction of single Rab13 RNAs, these results additionally indicate that containment within clusters is not required for silencing but might be a consequence of it.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that single RNAs in retracting protrusions are also silent.

claims.claim: In MDA-MB-231 cells, 29.7 ± 4.6% of protrusions contained clusters of Rab13 RNA without any corresponding accumulation of polyA RNA signal.
claims.source: Examination of multiple protrusions revealed that 29.7 ± 4.6% of protrusions (n = 60) contained clusters of Rab13 RNA without any corresponding accumulation of polyA RNA signal, while in 27.9 ± 6.4% of protrusions Rab13 RNA appeared to be part of more heterogenous, polyA-positive assemblies.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9D quantifying different types of RNA clusters.

claims.claim: In MDA-MB-231 cells, 27.9 ± 6.4% of protrusions contained Rab13 RNA that appeared to be part of more heterogenous, polyA-positive assemblies.
claims.source: Examination of multiple protrusions revealed that 29.7 ± 4.6% of protrusions (n = 60) contained clusters of Rab13 RNA without any corresponding accumulation of polyA RNA signal, while in 27.9 ± 6.4% of protrusions Rab13 RNA appeared to be part of more heterogenous, polyA-positive assemblies.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9D quantifying different types of RNA clusters.

claims.claim: MDA-MB-231 cells form a spectrum of clusters of different sizes.
claims.source: Considering that polyA intensity is reflective of the amount of contained RNAs, it therefore appears that MDA-MB-231 cells form a spectrum of clusters of different sizes.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of different types of clusters with varying polyA content.

claims.claim: The observed differences in cluster composition between cell types likely reflect the dynamics of these granules.
claims.source: Given that the lifetimes of retracting protrusions are noticeably different in the two cell types (with NIH/3T3 protrusions persisting for a longer time, while MDA-MB-231 protrusions quickly retracting within a few minutes; compare Videos 11 and 12 to Video 13), a likely possibility is that the observed differences reflect the dynamics of these granules (see discussion).
claims.evidence: This is speculation based on the correlation between protrusion dynamics and cluster composition.

claims.claim: In mouse fibroblast cells, the local concentration of polyA RNA at protrusions is a more reliable identifier of peripheral RNA clusters compared to the detection of any one particular RNA species that constitutes them.
claims.source: Indeed, in these cells, the local concentration of polyA RNA at protrusions is a more reliable identifier of peripheral RNA clusters compared to the detection of any one particular RNA species that constitutes them.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that polyA signal is more consistently associated with clusters than individual RNA species.

claims.claim: For low-abundance RNAs such as Pkp4, a large proportion of protrusions exhibit visible polyA RNA clusters that either contain single Pkp4 RNA molecules (45.9%) or are devoid of Pkp4 RNA (41.8%).
claims.source: This is especially true in the case of low-abundance RNAs, such a Pkp4, for which a large proportion of protrusions exhibit visible polyA RNA clusters that either contain single Pkp4 RNA molecules (Figure 10—figure supplement 1; white arrows; 45.9% (n = 98)), or are devoid of Pkp4 RNA (Figure 10—figure supplement 1; yellow arrowheads; 41.8% (n = 98)).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 1 quantifying Pkp4 presence in polyA clusters.

claims.claim: 25–30% of protrusions contain peripheral polyA granules.
claims.source: Scoring of cell populations for the presence of polyA granules at protrusions revealed that 25–30% of protrusions contain peripheral polyA granules (Figure 10).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 10 quantifying the presence of polyA granules.

claims.claim: Inhibition of translation doesn't disrupt the formation of peripheral polyA granules.
claims.source: Interestingly, inhibition of translation doesn't disrupt their formation, contrasting with the behavior exhibited by other types of cytoplasmic RNA granules, such as stress granules, which are rapidly dissolved upon inhibition of translation elongation.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 10 showing persistence of granules after translation inhibition.

claims.claim: Brief treatment with cycloheximide or puromycin promotes the appearance of peripheral polyA granules.
claims.source: Instead, for peripheral polyA granules, brief treatment with cycloheximide or puromycin promotes their appearance (Figure 10), suggesting that translational inhibition is a limiting step in the formation of RNA clusters at protrusions.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 10 showing increased granule formation after translation inhibition.

claims.claim: Translational inhibition is a limiting step in the formation of RNA clusters at protrusions.
claims.source: Instead, for peripheral polyA granules, brief treatment with cycloheximide or puromycin promotes their appearance (Figure 10), suggesting that translational inhibition is a limiting step in the formation of RNA clusters at protrusions.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that translation inhibitors promote granule formation.

claims.claim: Disruption of microtubules with nocodazole significantly reduced the appearance of polyA RNA granules at protrusions.
claims.source: Even looking at this narrower group of cells revealed that disruption of microtubules, or detyrosinated microtubules, significantly reduced the appearance of polyA RNA granules at protrusions (Figure 10).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 10 showing reduced granule formation after nocodazole treatment.

claims.claim: Disruption of detyrosinated microtubules with parthenolide significantly reduced the appearance of polyA RNA granules at protrusions.
claims.source: Even looking at this narrower group of cells revealed that disruption of microtubules, or detyrosinated microtubules, significantly reduced the appearance of polyA RNA granules at protrusions (Figure 10).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 10 showing reduced granule formation after parthenolide treatment.

claims.claim: Peripheral RNA granules result from, and require, RNA transport to the periphery.
claims.source: These results, together with the data presented above, are consistent with the model that peripheral RNA granules result from, and require, RNA transport to the periphery.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing that disrupting transport reduces granule formation.

claims.claim: The mode of regulation of APC-dependent RNAs is distinct from the one proposed for several other localized transcripts.
claims.source: This mode of regulation is distinct from the one proposed for several other localized transcripts, whereby RNAs are transported in a silenced state and are translationally activated only upon reaching the final destination or upon receipt of specific signals (Besse and Ephrussi, 2008; Buxbaum et al., 2015; Jung et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the findings of this study to the established model in the literature.

claims.claim: The proteins encoded by APC-dependent RNAs can be produced in internal regions without deleterious effects.
claims.source: Our observation of translation regardless of cytoplasmic location suggests that the proteins encoded by APC-dependent RNAs can be produced in internal regions without deleterious effects.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that APC-dependent RNAs are translated in both internal and peripheral locations.

claims.claim: Translation in local environments can attribute proteins with different properties.
claims.source: We propose that this mode of regulation could additionally have functional implications for the encoded proteins. Specifically, translation in local environments can attribute proteins with different properties.
claims.evidence: This is speculation about the potential functional implications of the observed regulation.

claims.claim: A single mRNA, as it is being continuously translated at various stages during its transport to the periphery, could give rise to protein copies which have different properties depending on the local micro-environment they are translated into.
claims.source: In light of these ideas, we suggest that a single mRNA, as it is being continuously translated at various stages during its transport to the periphery, could give rise to protein copies which have different properties, and therefore functional potential, depending on the local micro-environment they are translated into.
claims.evidence: This is speculation about the potential functional implications of the observed regulation.

claims.claim: Translation of APC-dependent RNAs is specifically suppressed in retracting protrusions and this silencing is associated with the formation of multimeric heterogeneous clusters.
claims.source: We additionally show that translation of APC-dependent RNAs is specifically suppressed in retracting protrusions and this silencing is associated with the formation of multimeric heterogeneous clusters.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the main findings supported by experimental data in Figures 8 and 9.

claims.claim: Formation of peripheral RNA clusters is reduced by treatments that prevent RNA transport to the periphery and is increased upon global translational inhibition.
claims.source: Formation of these clusters is reduced by treatments that prevent RNA transport to the periphery and is increased upon global translational inhibition, suggesting that silencing is a limiting step in their formation.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of findings supported by experimental data in Figure 10.

claims.claim: Silencing is a limiting step in the formation of peripheral RNA clusters.
claims.source: Formation of these clusters is reduced by treatments that prevent RNA transport to the periphery and is increased upon global translational inhibition, suggesting that silencing is a limiting step in their formation.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that translation inhibition promotes cluster formation.

claims.claim: Silencing can occur outside of clusters, since a large proportion of RNAs are observed as single particles in retracting, translationally-silent protrusions.
claims.source: Nevertheless, silencing can occur outside of clusters, since a large proportion of RNAs are observed as single particles in retracting, translationally-silent protrusions.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing single RNAs in retracting protrusions.

claims.claim: The appearance of heterogenous RNA clusters at the tips of protrusions, and their relation to translation, are reminiscent of other types of RNA granules formed by liquid-liquid phase separation.
claims.source: The appearance of these heterogenous RNA clusters at the tips of protrusions, and their relation to translation, are reminiscent of other types of RNA granules formed by liquid-liquid phase separation (Courchaine et al., 2016; Weber and Brangwynne, 2012).
claims.evidence: This is a comparison to known properties of RNA granules, supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: In stress granules and processing bodies, translational silencing or decay can occur regardless of RNA localization within granules.
claims.source: For example, stress granules (SGs) and processing bodies (PBs) are sites of dynamic concentration of RNA molecules, but in both cases translational silencing or decay can occur regardless of RNA localization within granules (Halstead et al., 2015; Panas et al., 2016; Perez-Pepe et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature describing properties of stress granules and P-bodies.

claims.claim: Stress granules and processing bodies form throughout the cytoplasm under normal conditions or in response to stress.
claims.source: SGs and PBs form throughout the cytoplasm under normal conditions or in response to stress.
claims.evidence: This represents established knowledge about stress granules and P-bodies.

claims.claim: The assembly/disassembly of peripheral RNA clusters is controlled by spatial signals.
claims.source: An interesting distinction of the clusters described here is that their formation is induced in particular subcellular regions associated with protrusion retraction, suggesting that their assembly/disassembly is controlled by spatial signals.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that clusters form specifically at retracting protrusions.

claims.claim: Localization of APC-dependent RNAs to the periphery is important for cell migration.
claims.source: Given that localization of APC-dependent RNAs to the periphery is important for cell migration (Wang et al., 2017) these data could point to a functional role for spatially segregating translation such that local protein production occurs in actively extending regions, while being suppressed in retracting areas.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work from the authors' laboratory.

claims.claim: The spatial segregation of translation could have a functional role such that local protein production occurs in actively extending regions, while being suppressed in retracting areas.
claims.source: Given that localization of APC-dependent RNAs to the periphery is important for cell migration (Wang et al., 2017) these data could point to a functional role for spatially segregating translation such that local protein production occurs in actively extending regions, while being suppressed in retracting areas.
claims.evidence: This is speculation about the potential functional implications of the observed regulation.

claims.claim: There exists a dynamic regulatory mechanism that coordinates APC-dependent RNA translation with the continuous protrusion and retraction cycles that characterize cellular migration.
claims.source: This would imply the existence of a dynamic regulatory mechanism that coordinates APC-dependent RNA translation with the continuous protrusion and retraction cycles that characterize cellular migration (Ji et al., 2008; Tkachenko et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism underlying the observed regulation, supported by citations to literature on cell migration dynamics.

claims.claim: A potential underlying mechanism for local silencing and granule formation could rely on spatially restricted phosphorylation/dephosphorylation events.
claims.source: A potential underlying mechanism for local silencing and granule formation could rely on spatially restricted phosphorylation/dephosphorylation events, which have been shown to affect the propensity of RNA-binding proteins to form phase-separated granules or to bind to RNAs (Monahan et al., 2017; Murray et al., 2017; Thapar, 2015).
claims.evidence: This is speculation about potential mechanisms, supported by citations to prior literature on phosphorylation effects on RNA granules.

claims.claim: Proteins associating with APC-dependent RNAs include the translational regulator FMRP and the RNA-binding protein FUS.
claims.source: In this regard, it is interesting that proteins associating with APC-dependent RNAs include the translational regulator FMRP and the RNA-binding protein FUS, one of the paradigm proteins used in understanding phase transitions (Mili et al., 2008; Yasuda et al., 2017; Yasuda et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work from the authors' laboratory.

claims.claim: Local modifications of FMRP or FUS could underlie the observed regulation.
claims.source: Local modifications of FMRP or FUS could underlie the observed regulation.
claims.evidence: This is speculation about potential mechanisms based on known properties of FMRP and FUS.

claims.claim: The extent of cluster formation might be influenced by the rate of retraction.
claims.source: However, our current data indicate that the extent of cluster formation might be influenced by the rate of retraction.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of cluster properties in different cell types with different retraction rates.

claims.claim: In NIH/3T3 cells, the majority of peripheral clusters are characterized by a visible accumulation of polyA signal, indicative of a high concentration of heterogeneous RNA species.
claims.source: Specifically, in NIH/3T3 cells, the majority of peripheral clusters are characterized by a visible accumulation of polyA signal, indicative of a high concentration of heterogeneous RNA species.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: Slowly retracting protrusions allow for the build-up of large heterogenous granules, while in faster retracting protrusions peripheral granules are transient, and rapidly disassemble either through RNA degradation or release into the cytosol.
claims.source: While we cannot rule out other interpretations, such as the existence of deadenylated transcripts, we favor the idea that slowly retracting protrusions allow for the build-up of large heterogenous granules, while in faster retracting protrusions peripheral granules are transient, and rapidly disassemble either through RNA degradation or release into the cytosol.
claims.evidence: This is speculation about the dynamics of granule assembly/disassembly based on the correlation with retraction rate.

claims.claim: Translationally silent, higher-order RNP complexes can sediment at sucrose density gradient fractions heavier than their translated counterparts.
claims.source: Translationally silent, higher-order RNP complexes can sediment at sucrose density gradient fractions heavier than their translated counterparts (Chekulaeva et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature describing sedimentation properties of RNP complexes.

claims.claim: The peripheral clusters of APC-dependent RNAs likely account for some of the RNA found at heavier fractions of the gradient.
claims.source: By analogy, the peripheral clusters of APC-dependent RNAs likely account for some of the RNA found at heavier fractions of the gradient.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the known sedimentation properties of RNA granules.

claims.claim: Reduction of peripheral cluster formation upon parthenolide treatment could likely account for the apparent shift of APC-dependent RNAs towards the lighter polysome fraction of the gradient.
claims.source: Reduction of their formation upon parthenolide treatment (Figure 10) could likely account for the apparent shift of APC-dependent RNAs towards the lighter polysome fraction of the gradient (Figures 1D and 2B).
claims.evidence: This is an inference connecting the reduction in cluster formation to the observed shift in polysome distribution.

claims.claim: APC-dependent RNAs can be found in internal cytoplasmic granules induced by expression of FUS mutants carrying ALS-associated mutations.
claims.source: We had previously reported that APC-dependent RNAs can also be found in internal cytoplasmic granules induced by expression of FUS mutants carrying ALS-associated mutations.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work from the authors' laboratory (Yasuda et al., 2013).

claims.claim: In FUS-granules APC-dependent RNAs are translationally active.
claims.source: Intriguingly, in these FUS-granules APC-dependent RNAs are translationally active (Yasuda et al., 2013).

claims.claim: For APC-dependent RNAs, their physical partitioning into granules is not the sole determinant, but acts in combination with the particular local environment to determine the eventual impact on their translation status.
claims.source: Taken together, these observations raise the possibility that, at least for APC-dependent RNAs, their physical partitioning into granules is not the sole determinant, but acts in combination with the particular local environment to determine the eventual impact on their translation status.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that APC-dependent RNAs have different translation states in different types of granules.

results.result: Puromycin treatment validates the polysome gradient fractionation method by causing dissociation of polysomes and shifting RNA distribution from heavy polysome fractions (3 and 4) to lighter fractions (1 and 2), confirming that fractions 3 and 4 contain actively translated transcripts.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C35 provide methodological validation through puromycin treatment showing expected polysome dissociation (C33), quantitative RNA redistribution across all RNA groups (C34), and correct interpretation that fractions 3/4 represent active translation (C35). The data in Figure 1B-D directly support these conclusions.

results.result: Disrupting peripheral localization of APC-dependent RNAs through either competitive UTR overexpression or parthenolide-mediated disruption of detyrosinated microtubules does not significantly affect their translational efficiency, suggesting lack of coupling between RNA transport and translational control.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C41 demonstrate that two independent methods of disrupting RNA localization (cUTR competition and parthenolide treatment) both reduce peripheral RNA enrichment (C36-C38) without affecting polysome profiles (C39) or translation state of the analyzed RNAs (C40). The conclusion of uncoupled transport and translation (C41) is well-supported by Figures 1C-D and 2A-B, though the authors note small non-significant shifts in heavy polysome fractions that may warrant further investigation.

results.result: The SunTag-based translation reporter system enables single-molecule visualization of RNA and nascent protein in live cells, with validation showing specific detection of RNA molecules via PP7-mCherry and active translation via GFP signal that is sensitive to translation inhibitors.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C49 establish the SunTag reporter system with appropriate controls. RNA detection specificity is validated by comparing +PP7 vs -PP7 constructs (C46-C47), translation signal is confirmed by puromycin sensitivity (C48), and active translation is distinguished from stalled ribosomes using harringtonine/lactimidomycin vs cycloheximide (C49). Figure 3 and supplementary data provide comprehensive validation.

results.result: Localized translation reporters carrying Rab13 or Pkp4 UTRs show peripheral enrichment with ~50% of molecules within 3-7 μm of cell edge, exist predominantly as single molecules, and exhibit mostly static or oscillatory motion with a small subset showing directed movement.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C56 characterize reporter RNA distribution and dynamics. Peripheral enrichment is quantified (C50-C51), single-molecule status confirmed by intensity distributions (C52), and detection limitations acknowledged (C53-C54). Motion characteristics are described from live imaging (C55-C56). Figure 4 and supplements provide supporting data, though the authors appropriately note limitations in detecting fast-moving molecules.

results.result: Translation efficiency of APC-dependent RNAs is independent of their distance from the cell periphery, with Pearson correlation coefficients near zero for all reporters, and some RNAs can be translated while undergoing directed movement.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C59 present the key finding that translation efficiency is uncorrelated with position (r ≈ 0 for all reporters), supported by Figure 4A data. Claims C60-C61 provide additional observation of translation during transport, though the authors appropriately note this is too infrequent for definitive conclusions. The main conclusion of position-independent translation is well-supported.

results.result: Endogenous APC-dependent RNAs exist in two states: as single molecules or as heterogeneous clusters containing multiple RNA species at the tips of protrusions in a 2μm peripheral region, with clusters overlapping polyA RNA accumulations and representing only a small fraction of total RNA in a subset of protrusions.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C73 comprehensively characterize peripheral RNA clusters. FISH intensity quantification confirms multiple RNAs per cluster (C67), co-localization experiments show heterogeneity (C68-C69), and low individual RNA copy numbers support the inference of additional species in polyA-positive clusters (C70-C71). The spatial specificity is demonstrated by comparison to non-localized RNAs (C73). Figure 5 and supplements provide extensive supporting data.

results.result: The clustering behavior of endogenous APC-dependent RNAs is recapitulated by exogenous reporter RNAs carrying Rab13 or Net1 3'UTRs, with live imaging showing smaller RNA particles trafficking toward and incorporating into larger peripheral clusters, demonstrating that clustering is mediated by 3'UTR signals.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C77 extend the clustering observations to reporter systems. MS2-tagged reporters show similar clustering patterns (C74-C75), live imaging directly demonstrates RNA incorporation into clusters (C76), and the conclusion that 3'UTRs mediate this behavior (C77) is well-supported by Figure 5 supplement 3 and Videos 7-8.

results.result: Translation reporters at protrusion tips form RNA clusters that are translationally silent, as measured by reduced GFP/mCherry ratios, leading to the conclusion that while APC-dependent RNAs are translated with similar efficiency in internal and peripheral locations, a subset at protrusion tips coalesces into translationally silent clusters.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C82 demonstrate translational silencing in peripheral clusters using the SunTag reporters. The reduced GFP/mCherry ratio in clustered vs single RNAs (C80) provides direct evidence of silencing. The synthesis of findings (C81-C82) is well-supported by Figure 6 data, though the authors acknowledge clusters are less pronounced than endogenous due to brief induction (C79).

results.result: The puro-PLA assay specifically detects nascent Rab13 protein in primary human dermal fibroblasts, revealing approximately 40 translation sites per cell that match the ~40-50 Rab13 RNA molecules detected by FISH, indicating a large fraction of Rab13 RNAs are actively translated, with translation occurring in both peripheral and perinuclear locations.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C90 validate the puro-PLA method and apply it to endogenous Rab13. Specificity is confirmed by knockdown and translation inhibitor controls (C83), CHX pretreatment distinguishes translation sites from released protein (C84-C85), and the agreement between translation sites and RNA copy numbers (C86-C88) supports high translation activity. Figure 7B-C provides supporting data.

results.result: Rab13 translation signal is less peripheral than Rab13 RNA signal and becomes progressively less peripheral over time during cell spreading, correlating with decreased spreading rate, suggesting peripheral translation is reduced as cells stop extending.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C97 reveal a temporal pattern in translation distribution. PDI measurements show translation is less peripheral than RNA (C91), this difference increases over time (C92-C93), and is not due to protein trafficking (C94). The correlation with spreading rate (C96-C97) provides mechanistic insight. Figure 7D-F supports these observations, though causality is not established.

results.result: In MDA-MB-231 cells, Rab13 RNA is present in both extending lamellipodia and retracting protrusions, but Rab13 translation is readily detected in lamellipodia and drastically reduced in retracting protrusions despite similar RNA levels, demonstrating that APC-dependent RNAs are translated in extending protrusions and silenced upon retraction.
results.evaluation: Claims C98-C107 resolve the paradox of peripheral silencing by identifying protrusion dynamics as the key variable. The characterization of retracting tails (C98-C100), validation of puro-PLA in MDA-MB-231 cells (C102), and quantification showing RNA presence but translation absence in retracting protrusions (C103-C106) provide strong evidence. Figure 8 comprehensively supports the conclusion that translation is coupled to protrusion extension/retraction (C107).

results.result: In MDA-MB-231 cells, Rab13 RNA exists predominantly as single molecules in lamellipodia but forms clusters of multiple molecules in retracting protrusions, with the presence of single silent RNAs in retracting protrusions indicating that clustering is not required for silencing but may be a consequence of it.
results.evaluation: Claims C108-C111 characterize RNA organization in different protrusion states. FISH intensity distributions distinguish single molecules in lamellipodia (C108) from clusters in retracting protrusions (C109). The inference that clustering is a consequence rather than cause of silencing (C111) is supported by the observation of single silent RNAs (C110). Figure 9B-C provides supporting data.

results.result: MDA-MB-231 retracting protrusions contain a spectrum of Rab13 RNA cluster types, with ~30% showing Rab13 clusters without polyA accumulation and ~28% showing heterogeneous polyA-positive assemblies, with differences between cell types likely reflecting granule dynamics related to retraction speed.
results.evaluation: Claims C112-C114 quantify cluster heterogeneity in MDA-MB-231 cells, showing a spectrum of cluster sizes. The speculation about dynamics (C115) is appropriately presented as a possibility based on observed differences in retraction kinetics between cell types. Figure 9D and comparison with NIH/3T3 cells support these observations.

results.result: In NIH/3T3 cells, 25-30% of protrusions contain peripheral polyA granules that are more reliably detected than individual RNA species; these granules are not disrupted by translation inhibition but are promoted by cycloheximide/puromycin treatment and reduced by microtubule disruption, indicating they result from RNA transport and that translational inhibition is a limiting step in their formation.
results.evaluation: Claims C116-C124 characterize peripheral granule formation requirements. The use of polyA as a cluster marker is justified (C116-C117), quantification establishes baseline frequency (C118), and the differential effects of translation inhibitors vs microtubule disruptors (C119-C123) support the model that transport is required and silencing promotes cluster formation (C121, C124). Figure 10 and supplement provide comprehensive supporting data.

results.result: The translational regulation of APC-dependent RNAs differs from the canonical model of transport-coupled silencing, with proteins being produced in internal regions without deleterious effects, and the authors propose that translation in different local environments could generate protein copies with different properties depending on the local microenvironment.
results.evaluation: Claim C125 is well-supported by the data showing position-independent translation. However, claims C126-C128 are speculative proposals about functional implications. While the speculation is reasonable and grounded in literature about co-translational processes, there is no direct experimental evidence in this study that proteins translated in different locations have different properties or that this has functional consequences.

results.result: Translation of APC-dependent RNAs is suppressed in retracting protrusions with associated formation of multimeric heterogeneous clusters; cluster formation is reduced by preventing RNA transport and increased by translational inhibition, with silencing occurring both within and outside clusters.
results.evaluation: Claims C129-C132 synthesize the major findings. The suppression in retracting protrusions and cluster formation (C129) is supported by Figures 8-9. The effects of transport disruption and translation inhibition on cluster formation (C130-C131) are supported by Figure 10. The observation that silencing can occur outside clusters (C132) is supported by Figure 9 showing single silent RNAs.

results.result: Peripheral RNA clusters share properties with phase-separated RNA granules like stress granules and P-bodies, but are distinguished by spatial control of their assembly/disassembly in specific subcellular regions associated with protrusion retraction.
results.evaluation: Claims C133-C136 contextualize the findings within the RNA granule literature. The comparison to phase-separated granules (C133) and stress granules/P-bodies (C134-C135) is supported by appropriate citations. The distinction of spatial control (C136) is a reasonable inference from the data showing clusters specifically at retracting protrusions.

results.result: Given that APC-dependent RNA localization is important for cell migration, the spatial segregation of translation between extending and retracting regions could have a functional role, implying a dynamic regulatory mechanism coordinating translation with protrusion/retraction cycles.
results.evaluation: Claim C137 about the importance of RNA localization for migration is supported by prior work (citation). However, claims C138-C139 about functional roles and regulatory mechanisms are speculative. While the speculation is reasonable and well-motivated by the data, no functional experiments are performed to test whether the observed translation regulation actually impacts migration or protein function.

results.result: Spatially restricted phosphorylation/dephosphorylation events could underlie local silencing and granule formation, potentially involving local modifications of FMRP or FUS, which are known to associate with APC-dependent RNAs.
results.evaluation: Claims C140-C142 propose potential mechanisms. While FMRP and FUS association with APC-dependent RNAs is supported by prior work (C141), the proposals about phosphorylation-mediated regulation (C140) and local modifications (C142) are speculative. These are reasonable hypotheses based on literature about RNA granule regulation, but no experimental evidence is provided in this study.

results.result: The extent of cluster formation may be influenced by retraction rate, with slowly retracting NIH/3T3 protrusions showing large heterogeneous polyA-positive granules, while faster retracting MDA-MB-231 protrusions may have more transient granules that rapidly disassemble.
results.evaluation: Claims C143-C145 propose a model for cluster dynamics. The observation of different cluster compositions between cell types (C144) is supported by Figures 5 and 9. However, the proposed relationship to retraction rate (C143, C145) is speculative, based on correlation rather than experimental manipulation of retraction speed. Alternative explanations (e.g., deadenylated transcripts) are acknowledged but not tested.

results.result: Peripheral RNA clusters likely account for some APC-dependent RNA found in heavier gradient fractions, and reduction of cluster formation by parthenolide could explain the apparent shift toward lighter polysome fractions observed in the gradient experiments.
results.evaluation: Claims C146-C148 provide a mechanistic explanation for the subtle gradient shifts noted earlier. The principle that silent RNP complexes sediment in heavier fractions (C146) is supported by literature. The inference that peripheral clusters contribute to heavy fractions (C147) and that their reduction explains the parthenolide effect (C148) is reasonable and connects observations from Figures 1-2 with Figure 10.

results.result: APC-dependent RNAs in FUS-mutant-induced internal granules are translationally active, contrasting with their silencing in peripheral clusters, suggesting that physical partitioning into granules is not the sole determinant of translation status but acts in combination with local environment.
results.evaluation: Claims C149-C151 integrate prior findings from the authors' laboratory with current results. The observation of active translation in FUS granules (C149-C150) is supported by citation to prior work. The inference about context-dependent effects of granule partitioning (C151) is reasonable given the contrasting translation states in different granule types, though mechanistic understanding is limited.
